ocar.opportunity: High-resolution electron microscopy can resolve synapses and thin processes such as dendritic spines, but reconstructing those processes from huge EM volumes is slow if every slice must be traced by hand.
ocar.challenge: EM datasets are too large and cluttered for interactive viewing and segmentation with then-standard tools, and neural processes can be extremely narrow (spines of roughly 50 nm) while z-slice spacing is large.
ocar.action: Jeong, Beyer, Hadwiger, Vazquez, Pfister, and Whitaker, in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2009), introduce NeuroTrace: GPU-based semi-automatic multiphase level-set segmentation with 3D tracking, plus volume rendering that does view-dependent filtering, a local-histogram edge metric, and on-the-fly implicit-surface ray-casting.
ocar.resolution: A comparison with a commonly used manual EM segmentation tool found the NeuroTrace workflow faster and easier for reconstructing complex neural processes. Collaborators in the Lichtman and Reid groups were using the system; a user study included members of those labs.
ocar.future_work: The authors want more filters and automatic opacity settings, interpolation to handle large z-gaps, tracking through merges and branches, and simultaneous tracking of many processes on a GPU cluster.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are huge and hard to trace by hand. NeuroTrace is an early interactive computer tool that helps people follow nerve fibers through those pictures in 3D.
summaries.intermediate: Jeong and colleagues (IEEE TVCG, 2009) present NeuroTrace, a GPU system for semi-automatic segmentation and visualization of neural processes in EM volumes. Segmentation uses a multiphase level set with 3D tracking; rendering uses on-demand filtering, a local-histogram edge metric, and ray-cast implicit surfaces of segmented structures. They report that the interactive workflow is faster and easier than a then-common manual EM segmentation tool. The extract is an NIH author manuscript of the published paper, citing collaborators Jeff Lichtman and Clay Reid.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2009 methods/systems paper, not a completed dense reconstruction. The extract does not quantify speedup or error rates beyond a qualitative user-study comparison. Spine diameter (~50 nm) is given as motivation for EM resolution. Future-work items (branching, z-gap interpolation) indicate the tracker as published did not yet handle merges and branches. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are huge and hard to trace by hand. NeuroTrace is an early interactive computer tool that helps people follow nerve fibers through those pictures in 3D.

ocar.opportunity: Complete circuit maps had been obtained only in C. elegans. A tractable mammalian circuit would show whether similar organizational principles hold when neurons are not uniquely identified.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian nervous systems are too large to reconstruct wholesale; pooling partial data across animals assumes class-level homogeneity that may be false.
ocar.action: Lu, Tapia, White, and Lichtman, in PLoS Biology (2009), reconstruct the motor-axon innervation of six interscutularis muscles from adult transgenic mice with fluorescent proteins in all motor axons, using automated optical microscopy and computer-assisted analysis.
ocar.resolution: The maps give an anatomical correlate of Henneman’s size principle, a quantitative link among axonal caliber, length, and synapse number, substantial left–right structural variation unlike invertebrate identified neurons, and axons whose paths are often longer than necessary (about 6% branch extramuscularly). The authors attribute variability to synaptic competition.
ocar.future_work: They anticipate similar imaging for CNS connectomes but note denser neuropil and smaller length scales will require spectral labeling, super-resolution, serial sectioning, adaptive optics, or clearing, plus more automated reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Only the worm had a complete wiring diagram of a circuit. This team maps every motor nerve and muscle fiber in a small mouse ear muscle and finds the wiring is variable, not a neat shortest-path plan.
summaries.intermediate: Lu, Tapia, White, and Lichtman (PLoS Biology, 2009) reconstruct connectomes of six adult mouse interscutularis muscles labeled with fluorescent proteins in all motor axons. They report an anatomical basis for the size principle, a robust relationship among axon caliber, length, and synapse number, left–right differences in the same animal, and wiring lengths often longer than necessary. They contrast this variability with stereotyped identified neurons in invertebrates and argue synaptic competition shapes the final diagram. This is an optical neuromuscular map, not an EM CNS connectome.
summaries.advanced: Six muscles from adult transgenic mice; the ~6% extramuscular branching figure is from the extract’s discussion. ‘Connectome’ here means the complete motor-unit innervation of one muscle, not a brain volume. Comparison to C. elegans is conceptual. CNS generalization is prospective. Counts of axons or fibers per muscle are not summarized as a single number in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Only the worm had a complete wiring diagram of a circuit. This team maps every motor nerve and muscle fiber in a small mouse ear muscle and finds the wiring is variable, not a neat shortest-path plan.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely supplies both a synaptic wiring diagram and gene-expression signatures for most neurons, so one can test whether genetics predict who connects to whom at nervous-system scale.
ocar.challenge: Classic genetics had identified many pathfinding genes, but not a large-scale quantitative link between a neuron’s expression signature and its specific partners.
ocar.action: Kaufman, Dror, Meilijson, and Ruppin, in PLoS Computational Biology (2006), combine White/Durbin connectivity with WormBase expression and apply two complementary assays plus feature selection to ask whether expression predicts incoming and outgoing connectivity.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that a neuron’s expression signature carries significant information about its synaptic connectivity and produce a list of putative predictive genes, with the relation stronger in some neuron subsets. They treat the genes as candidates, not proven causal factors.
ocar.future_work: They stress that binary, noisy public data are crude relative to continuous expression and synapse weights, and they call for computational and experimental follow-up of the nominated genes (for example ceh-23, mps-1, and kvs-1).

summaries.beginner: In the worm, scientists already know both the wiring diagram and which genes many neurons express. This study asks whether a cell’s gene list can predict who it connects to, and finds that it can, at least in part.
summaries.intermediate: Kaufman, Dror, Meilijson, and Ruppin (PLoS Computational Biology, 2006) quantify the relationship between C. elegans neuronal gene-expression signatures (WormBase) and synaptic connectivity signatures (White et al. via Durbin). Two complementary assays indicate that expression carries significant information about connectivity and nominate putative genes. Feature selection is used to rank contributors; the authors warn that the public data are discrete and noisy. The paper is a computational analysis of existing maps, not a new reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: Connectivity is the classic White/Hall wiring (binary partners), not a modern reannotation with synapse weights. Expression is similarly binarized. Feature selection does not establish causality. Specific correlation values appear in figures rather than as a single summary statistic in the extract. Gene examples in the discussion (ceh-23, mps-1, kvs-1, gpa-3, che-2/3, osm-9/3) are putative.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, scientists already know both the wiring diagram and which genes many neurons express. This study asks whether a cell’s gene list can predict who it connects to, and finds that it can, at least in part.

ocar.opportunity: Whether individual CA3→CA1 axonal boutons can act as local compartments for synaptic efficacy and microconnectivity depends on their 3D shape, vesicle and mitochondrial content, and spacing.
ocar.challenge: Physiology had shown pre- and postsynaptic plasticity at Schaffer synapses, but serial-EM morphology of a nearly homogeneous CA3→CA1 axon population in stratum radiatum was incomplete.
ocar.action: Shepherd and Harris, in Journal of Neuroscience (1998), use serial EM in hippocampal slices to locate PSDs, vesicles, and mitochondria along 75 CA3→CA1 axon segments in mid-CA1 stratum radiatum, fully reconstructing eleven axons.
ocar.resolution: Synapses (PSD plus vesicles) occurred on average every 2.7 μm. Most varicosities (68%) had one PSD, 19% had 2–4, 13% had none; 90% contained vesicles; 53% lacked mitochondria and 8% contained only mitochondria. Varicosities varied greatly in length (1.1 ± 0.7 μm) and volume (0.13 ± 0.14 μm³); shafts were uniformly thin (0.17 ± 0.04 μm). Narrow shafts are argued to promote biochemical compartmentalization. Measurements are presented uncorrected for shrinkage.
ocar.future_work: The discussion flags convergence onto identified CA3–CA1 cell pairs and the heterogeneity of synaptic spacing (edge-to-edge PSD spacing varied more than 20-fold) as next questions; about 40% of PSDs sat on multiple-synapse boutons.

summaries.beginner: In the hippocampus, the axons that carry messages from CA3 to CA1 are not a string of identical beads. Serial electron microscopy shows boutons of many sizes, many without mitochondria, and thin necks that could keep each bouton chemically private.
summaries.intermediate: Shepherd and Harris (Journal of Neuroscience, 1998) reconstruct CA3→CA1 axons in rat hippocampal slices with serial EM. Along 75 segments (9.1 ± 2.0 μm), synapses defined by colocalized PSDs and vesicles occurred every 2.7 μm on average. Most varicosities had one PSD; about half lacked mitochondria. Eleven fully reconstructed axons showed oblong, highly variable varicosities and narrow, tubular shafts. The authors compare shafts to spine necks and raise the possibility of localized metabolic and connectivity differences among axons, varicosities, and synapses.
summaries.advanced: Tissue is hippocampal slices, not in vivo; measurements are uncorrected for unknown shrinkage (they discuss a 10–25% scenario). Synapse spacing 2.7 μm and component percentages are those stated in the paper. Light-microscopic inferences of ~20,000 synapses per CA3 cell in CA1 are cited from Andersen et al., not remeasured here. ‘CA33CA1’ in the extract is the CA3→CA1 arrow.

plain_language_summary: In the hippocampus, the axons that carry messages from CA3 to CA1 are not a string of identical beads. Serial electron microscopy shows boutons of many sizes, many without mitochondria, and thin necks that could keep each bouton chemically private.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric EM datasets now reach scales (a cubic millimeter can exceed a petabyte) that require shared high-performance computing, not only local workstations.
ocar.challenge: 3DEM labs need browser access to private and shared volumes, alignment and segmentation tools, and simulation environments, without each group standing up its own HPC stack.
ocar.action: Carson, Harris, Sejnowski and colleagues, in SN Computer Science (2026), describe 3dem.org, a TACC Core Experience Portal science gateway linked to Tapis for the NeuroNex 3DEM community.
ocar.resolution: The gateway offers browser access to raw and processed datasets, image-processing tools for alignment and segmentation, and simulation/analysis environments on TACC HPC, with a FAIR-oriented sharing model. The authors argue the template-gateway approach made initial customization available in less than a month and supports long-term updates via CEP/Tapis.
ocar.future_work: They note 3dem.org currently runs only on TACC-hosted resources; planned extensions include Tapis v3 automated workflows and optional external systems, plus community-driven feature priorities. Users considering external integrations must account for authentication and transfer time.

summaries.beginner: Three-dimensional electron-microscope volumes are now so large they need supercomputers. This paper describes a website, 3dem.org, that lets microscopy labs run that computing in a browser.
summaries.intermediate: Carson et al. (SN Computer Science, 2026) present 3dem.org, a science gateway built from the Texas Advanced Computing Center Core Experience Portal and Tapis API. It gives the 3DEM community browser access to private and shared volumes, alignment and segmentation tools, and simulation environments on TACC HPC. A cubic millimeter exceeding one petabyte is given as scale motivation. Discussion emphasizes FAIR stewardship, versioned public datasets, containerized workflows, and template-gateway sustainability across NeuroNex-related users.
summaries.advanced: This is infrastructure/systems reporting, not a new reconstruction or benchmarked segmentation algorithm. The ‘less than a month’ customization claim is the authors’ deployment narrative. Current operation is TACC-only despite Tapis supporting external systems. Dataset sizes and user counts are not given as a single census in the extract. NSF DBI-1707356 and DBI-2014862 funded the work.

plain_language_summary: Three-dimensional electron-microscope volumes are now so large they need supercomputers. This paper describes a website, 3dem.org, that lets microscopy labs run that computing in a browser.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a fully mapped connectome, a short lifespan, and extensive gene homology with humans, so it can be used to study neuronal aging and neurodegeneration at circuit and molecular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian neurodegeneration is slow and cell-biologically complex; a simpler animal is needed to dissect conserved pathways and to screen drugs and stressors, including hypoxia.
ocar.action: Pan, Shen, Peng, Tang, Ran, Liu, Zeng, and Liu, in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience (2026), review C. elegans as a neuroscience and disease-modeling organism, covering neural communication architecture, molecular disease models, pharmacological screening, toxicology, and genomics.
ocar.resolution: The review presents the worm’s quantifiable behaviors, genetic tractability, and mapped connectome as a framework for studying neurodegenerative mechanisms and translational questions under stress, particularly hypoxia. Keywords center on Alzheimer’s disease, synaptic transmission, and model-organism utility.
ocar.future_work: As a review it does not generate new maps; it positions the system for further screening and clinical-translation hypotheses rather than claiming a specific therapeutic result.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram and genes that often match ours. This review explains how scientists use that simple nervous system to study aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s.
summaries.intermediate: Pan et al. (Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience, 2026) review C. elegans as a model for neuronal aging and neurodegeneration. They emphasize a fully mapped connectome, short lifespan, conserved pathways, and quantifiable behavior, then survey neural communication, molecular disease models, high-throughput pharmacology, environmental toxicology, and genomic tools. Hypoxia is highlighted as a stress condition of translational interest. The piece is a narrative review, not a new connectome or primary disease experiment.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; disease-model and screening claims are synthesized from cited literature. The extract’s later pages are layout-noisy (mixed table fragments), so mechanistic details should be checked in the formatted article. ‘Fully mapped connectome’ is the standard worm claim, not a new reconstruction here.

plain_language_summary: The roundworm C. elegans has a complete wiring diagram and genes that often match ours. This review explains how scientists use that simple nervous system to study aging and diseases such as Alzheimer’s.

ocar.opportunity: Self-righting when turned upside-down is a stereotyped postural behavior, but the sensory-to-motor circuit that implements it along the body axis had not been mapped in any animal.
ocar.challenge: Larval Drosophila self-righting depends on segmentally repeated LT1/2 motor neurons and Hox-targeting microRNAs, yet the upstream sensory and interneuron architecture across abdominal segments was unresolved.
ocar.action: Picao-Osorio, Roseby, Hancock, Cardona, and Alonso, in a July 2026 bioRxiv preprint, combine connectomic reconstruction from a first-instar EM volume with thermogenetic silencing to trace and test the self-righting circuit along the antero-posterior axis.
ocar.resolution: Starting from LT1/2 motor neurons they identify premotor interneurons, upstream partners, and class IV multidendritic sensory neurons as core elements; silencing most of these impairs self-righting. The circuit overlaps nociceptive rolling and touch crawling at shared interneurons including DnB, A02o (Wave-1), and TePn05. Network analyses show nested hubs, a few integrator neurons, and declining synapse number and density toward posterior segments.
ocar.future_work: Several elements were reconstructed in only a subset of segments, and analysis is restricted to one first-instar EM volume, so axial trends are a first approximation. They suggest dissecting computations at integrator nodes, linking Hox-regulated microRNAs to this wiring, and informing axial control in soft robotics.

summaries.beginner: When a fruit-fly maggot is flipped on its back, it rights itself with a stereotyped twist. This preprint maps the nerve cells for that maneuver along the body and shows the circuit shares parts with rolling and crawling.
summaries.intermediate: Picao-Osorio et al. (bioRxiv, posted 27 July 2026) reconstruct the Drosophila larval self-righting circuit from EM connectomics and test components by thermogenetic silencing. Core elements include LT1/2 motor neurons, premotor interneurons (A18j, A01c, A14a, A26f among those named in the conclusion), class IV md sensory neurons, and shared rolling/crawling interneurons DnB, A02o (Wave-1), and TePn05. They report nested hub organization, a few sensory–motor integrators, and an antero-posterior decline in synapse number and density. They call this the first axial wiring diagram of a postural control circuit.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint based on a single first-instar EM volume (Ohyama/Schneider-Mizell lineage). Not all neurons were reconstructed in every segment. ‘Great majority’ of identified components affect self-righting when silenced; the extract does not tabulate exact n per cell type in the truncated text. Overlap with rolling/crawling is structural plus behavioral impairment, not a full competition model.

plain_language_summary: When a fruit-fly maggot is flipped on its back, it rights itself with a stereotyped twist. This preprint maps the nerve cells for that maneuver along the body and shows the circuit shares parts with rolling and crawling.

ocar.opportunity: Deep-learning neuron segmentation in EM needs more diverse labeled volumes than labs can paint by hand; synthetic image–label pairs could stretch scarce annotations.
ocar.challenge: Geometric and photometric augmentations stay highly correlated with the original images and add little structural diversity.
ocar.action: Jiang, Zhang, Guo, Lu, Zhou, and Han, in IEEE ISBI (2026; extract is arXiv:2601.15779), propose a diffusion-based augmentation framework: a resolution-aware conditional diffusion model synthesizes voxels from 3D masks, plus a biology-guided mask-remodeling module.
ocar.resolution: On AC3 and AC4 under low-annotation regimes, they report ARAND improvements of 32.1% and 30.7% when the method is combined with two different post-processing methods. Code is released as NeuroDiff.
ocar.future_work: The extract is a short conference-style paper; broader generalization beyond AC3/AC4 and other post-processors is left to users of the released code.

summaries.beginner: Teaching computers to trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually needs lots of hand-drawn labels. This team uses a diffusion model to invent extra realistic training images so the tracer can learn from fewer real labels.
summaries.intermediate: Jiang et al. (IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging, 2026; arXiv extract dated 22 January 2026) describe NeuroDiff, a conditional diffusion augmenter for EM neuron segmentation. A resolution-aware model with multi-scale conditioning and EM resolution priors synthesizes images from 3D masks; a biology-guided module remodels masks. On AC3 and AC4 in low-annotation settings they report 32.1% and 30.7% ARAND gains with two post-processing methods. Traditional geometric/photometric augmentation is the baseline they argue against.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF is an arXiv preprint of the ISBI paper (conference DOI not printed in the extract). ARAND improvements are those stated for AC3/AC4 under low-annotation regimes combined with two post-processors named in the full paper; check annotation fractions there. Code: github.com/HeadLiuYun/NeuroDiff. Catalog author ‘Rui Zhou’ appears as ‘Ruining Zhou’ on the PDF.

plain_language_summary: Teaching computers to trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually needs lots of hand-drawn labels. This team uses a diffusion model to invent extra realistic training images so the tracer can learn from fewer real labels.

ocar.opportunity: Alzheimer disease still lacks a definitive cure; seeing subcellular pathology at high resolution is needed to link plaques, tangles, and organelle damage to mechanism and to drug design.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy cannot resolve the ultrastructure of amyloid deposits, paired helical filaments, synapses, mitochondria, or the blood–brain barrier, and fixation can itself create artifacts.
ocar.action: Dallere, Migheli, and Vercelli, in Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology (2026), review electron microscopy of AD from 1960s TEM/SEM through volume EM, cryo-EM, cryo-ET, and CLEM, covering human tissue, animal models, cultures, and synthetic assemblies.
ocar.resolution: They argue EM remains indispensable: Terry and Kidd established Aβ and PHF ultrastructure; later vEM, cryo-EM, and cryo-ET add 3D, near-native, and near-atomic views of synapses, mitochondria, lysosomes, BBB, iron, and inflammation. Cross-system comparison is presented as a way to find conserved pathological features and to guide therapeutic molecules.
ocar.future_work: As a review it does not report a new volume; translational claims are prospective. Readers should treat graphical-abstract categories (plaques, tau, synapses, mitochondria, inflammation, autophagy, BBB, iron) as a map of the literature, not a single experiment.

summaries.beginner: Alzheimer disease changes cells in ways too small for ordinary microscopes. This review traces how electron microscopy, from the 1960s to modern 3D and cryo methods, has shown plaques, tangles, and damaged organelles up close.
summaries.intermediate: Dallere, Migheli, and Vercelli (Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology, 2026) review EM in Alzheimer research. They start from Terry and Kidd’s ultrastructure of Aβ deposits and tau paired helical filaments and then cover TEM, SEM, volume EM, cryo-EM, cryo-ET, and CLEM in human brain, animals, cultures, and synthetic assemblies. They emphasize synapses, mitochondria, lysosomes, the blood–brain barrier, iron, and inflammatory machinery as EM-accessible compartments. The review is framed as both mechanistic synthesis and a guide to structure-based therapeutics.
summaries.advanced: Narrative review, not a primary reconstruction. Near-atomic claims refer to cryo-EM/ET literature, not a new structure determined here. Graphical abstract was created with BioRender. The extract’s later pages are reference-heavy; specific quantitative pathology metrics should be taken from the cited primary papers.

plain_language_summary: Alzheimer disease changes cells in ways too small for ordinary microscopes. This review traces how electron microscopy, from the 1960s to modern 3D and cryo methods, has shown plaques, tangles, and damaged organelles up close.

ocar.opportunity: If hub importance in one layer of a multilayer network predicts hubs in functionally similar layers, a single topological rule could be reused from molecular graphs to connectomes to software.
ocar.challenge: Prior multilayer work did not, on the authors’ account, isolate a pre-registered ‘functional proximity’ regularity with named boundary conditions across many domains.
ocar.action: Ivanov, an independent researcher, in an arXiv preprint (v8, June 2026; arXiv:2604.23639), reports 31 pre-registered experiments on a claimed Functional Proximity Law, including a Drosophila larval connectome test.
ocar.resolution: The author reports 25/31 confirmations (binomial p approximately 0.000439), nine canonical domains individually at p<0.05, six named boundary conditions, and a larval Drosophila connectome replication (n = 2952 neurons, Spearman ρ = 0.663, Pearson r = 0.363, p = 0.002). Limitations listed include exclusive use of degree centrality and small n in canonical experiments.
ocar.future_work: Proposed next steps include weighted and eigenvector hub persistence, a formal metric for functional proximity, and further pre-registered corpora. Several experiments use the author’s own IRDME codebase, which the limitations section flags as a possible circularity.

summaries.beginner: This preprint argues that important hubs in one layer of a network stay important in other, similar layers. One of the tests uses the fruit-fly larva wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: Ivanov (arXiv:2604.23639, June 2026 v8) proposes a Functional Proximity Law: hub importance persists more strongly between functionally similar multilayer-network layers than dissimilar ones. Across 31 pre-registered experiments the author reports 25 confirmations, six named structural boundary conditions, and a Drosophila melanogaster larval connectome test (n = 2952 neurons). Other claimed domains range from molecular biology and C. elegans to software and particle physics. The manuscript is an independent-researcher preprint, not a journal article.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint; treat p-values and confirmation counts as author-reported. Canonical experiments are described as small-n (n = 10 to 30) and retrospective; all use degree centrality. Functional proximity is classified by domain expertise, not a formal metric. Software experiments include the author’s IRDME tool as input (circularity flagged by the author). Connectome result is one of many tests, not a new reconstruction. Independent replication would be required before treating the ‘law’ as established.

plain_language_summary: This preprint argues that important hubs in one layer of a network stay important in other, similar layers. One of the tests uses the fruit-fly larva wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: The 302-neuron C. elegans hermaphrodite connectome is a compact example of adaptive, context-dependent behavior, while modern AI typically buys performance with scale rather than efficiency.
ocar.challenge: Deep networks need large labeled datasets, heavy compute, and extensive tuning, and they often fail to generalize or adapt without retraining.
ocar.action: Liu, Zheng, and Wang, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2026), mini-review studies that translate C. elegans circuit principles into artificial neural network architectures for machine control and image classification.
ocar.resolution: They highlight reported gains in robustness and performance when worm-inspired principles are built into ANNs, and they outline a path toward compact, adaptive, biologically inspired systems. The piece is a synthesis, not a new network trained by the authors.
ocar.future_work: The review points to further distillation of worm circuit principles for brain-inspired AI; it does not specify a single architecture as settled. Funding is NSFC 32371079.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system still produces flexible behavior. This short review asks what artificial intelligence could learn from that efficient wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Liu, Zheng, and Wang (Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 2026) review translations of C. elegans neural-circuit principles into artificial neural networks. They contrast the 302-neuron hermaphrodite connectome’s efficiency with scale-driven modern AI, then survey applications in machine control and image classification that report improved robustness. The article is a mini-review of existing studies, not a new connectome or a new benchmarked model from this group.
summaries.advanced: Mini-review; performance claims are those of the cited translation papers. ‘Simplest known nervous system’ and ‘302 neurons’ are the standard hermaphrodite figures. Authors state generative AI was not used in the manuscript. No new architecture or code is introduced here.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s tiny, fully mapped nervous system still produces flexible behavior. This short review asks what artificial intelligence could learn from that efficient wiring.

ocar.opportunity: In early retinitis pigmentosa, inner-retina rewiring may cause symptoms before photoreceptors are gone; a pathoconnectome plus a computational model could predict how Aii amacrine changes alter signaling.
ocar.challenge: Structural maps of degenerate retina do not by themselves show how new gap junctions and altered excitatory drive change bipolar, Aii, and ganglion-cell activity.
ocar.action: Iseri, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Anderson, Yang, Dahal, Garcia, Bouteiller, Jones, and Lazzi, in a bioRxiv preprint (DOI 2024.02.14; extract posted 5 May 2026), combine retinal pathoconnectome 1 (RPC1) with a computational model of the rewired rod pathway.
ocar.resolution: The model predicts changed bipolar and Aii EPSPs driven by newly formed gap junctions and rhythmic retinal ganglion cell firing of up to 10 Hz, consistent with network depolarization. The authors align this with patch-clamp in rd1 and rd10 mice and propose Aii-mediated alterations as a substrate for impaired photopic–scotopic adaptation. Simulations exploring rod convergence report a 10–25 Hz rhythmic range, saturating near 25 Hz at high rod convergence.
ocar.future_work: They suggest extending the model with multi-scale bioelectromagnetic simulations for neurostimulation, and they note pathoconnectome uncertainties (indeterminate photoreceptor synapses, species differences in rod convergence).

summaries.beginner: In a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration, the inner retina rewires as rods die. This preprint models how changes onto Aii amacrine cells can make ganglion cells fire in abnormal rhythms.
summaries.intermediate: Iseri et al. (bioRxiv; 2024.02.14 DOI, May 2026 version) analyze early retinal degeneration with pathoconnectome 1 and a computational rod-pathway model centered on glycinergic Aii amacrine cells. They report altered excitatory drive and gap-junction coupling of Aiis, model light-evoked EPSPs, and predict rhythmic RGC firing up to 10 Hz (10–25 Hz across rod-convergence simulations). Findings are compared with rd1/rd10 patch-clamp. The author summary frames the work as a realistic network model for cell replacement, optogenetics, and implants.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint (updated 2026). Firing-rate predictions are from a model constrained by RPC1, not a new EM volume. Many photoreceptor synapses were classified indeterminate; rod-convergence bounds include rabbit literature (~100 rods per RodBC) as an upper case. Alignment with rd1/rd10 is qualitative consistency, not a new physiology dataset in this extract. Catalog year is 2026; the DOI is the 2024 preprint identifier.

plain_language_summary: In a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration, the inner retina rewires as rods die. This preprint models how changes onto Aii amacrine cells can make ganglion cells fire in abnormal rhythms.

ocar.opportunity: Fly visual-system connectomes now cover whole optic lobes, so one can ask whether ‘the same’ cell type really wires the same way across columns.
ocar.challenge: Classical accounts treat repeating columns as translationally invariant units built from uniform cell types, yet regional and stochastic variation is also known.
ocar.action: Wernet and Silies, in BioEssays (2026), review connectomic evidence that cells assigned to one type vary in partner number, partner identity, and synapse counts, focusing on Drosophila vision.
ocar.resolution: They argue heterogeneous computations within defined cell types are the rule rather than the exception, and they pose whether that variability increases functional diversity or robustness. Peripheral examples include precise R1–R6 lamina wiring versus more divergent medulla pathways, with only 15 cell types described as truly columnar (once per medulla column) among many more downstream types.
ocar.future_work: The open question is functional: whether imprecise connectivity is noise, feature extraction, or a robustness mechanism. The review points to recently released female and male visual-system connectomes as the data to press that question.

summaries.beginner: Fly eyes look like a repeating grid of identical units, which should make vision the same everywhere. This essay uses wiring diagrams to argue that cells of one named type still differ in who they connect to.
summaries.intermediate: Wernet and Silies (BioEssays, 2026) review heterogeneity in Drosophila visual circuits in light of whole optic-lobe connectomes. They contrast the textbook picture of uniform, translationally invariant columns with connectomic reports that cells of one type vary in partners and synapse numbers. Lamina R1–R6 connectivity is described as extremely precise, while medulla pathways diverge; only 15 types are called truly columnar. The essay asks whether variable connectivity increases functional variability or robustness.
summaries.advanced: Review essay, not a new reconstruction. Columnar-type counts (15 of >50 downstream of L1–L5 in the extract) come from cited connectomes (e.g. recent female/male visual-system maps). Functional interpretations are explicitly open. Figure 1 notes BioRender and ChatGPT assistance for a schematic. Catalog journal spelling is Bioessays.

plain_language_summary: Fly eyes look like a repeating grid of identical units, which should make vision the same everywhere. This essay uses wiring diagrams to argue that cells of one named type still differ in who they connect to.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-mammalian-brain connectomics needs perfusion protocols that preserve ultrastructure, not only protocols that look well cleared on the bench or in a scanner.
ocar.challenge: Perfusion quality is often scored by gross appearance and neuroimaging of fixative distribution, which may not predict EM preservation when dehydrating agents are added.
ocar.action: Slaughter, Garrood, Hedden, Sowa, Janssen, Thorn, De Sanctis, Farrell, Crary, and McKenzie, in a July 2026 bioRxiv technical report, compare macroscopic/radiological perfusion metrics with EM in human and canine brains perfused with hyperosmotic additives.
ocar.resolution: In three human donors and one canine donor perfused with 10% mannitol plus 10% PEG 35 kDa, perfusion looked adequate or favorable macroscopically and radiologically, but EM showed expanded extracellular space, shrunken processes, and distorted membranes consistent with osmotic shock. Similar artifacts appeared in a canine brain with 20% mannitol in 20% NBF without PEG. Comparison cases used standard NBF without osmotic additives.
ocar.future_work: The report warns against optimizing connectomics perfusion on macroscopic or CT metrics alone. It does not propose a replacement recipe in the extract beyond that caution.

summaries.beginner: Flushing a brain with fixative can look successful from the outside or on a scan and still ruin the fine structure needed for wiring diagrams. This technical report shows that extra dehydrating chemicals can cause that mismatch.
summaries.intermediate: Slaughter et al. (bioRxiv, posted 30 July 2026) report that hyperosmotic brain perfusion can satisfy gross and radiological quality checks while destroying ultrastructure. Three human brains and one canine brain received 10% mannitol and 10% PEG 35 kDa; EM showed osmotic-shock artifacts. A canine case with 20% mannitol in 20% neutral buffered formalin without PEG was similar. They contrast these with previously reported standard-formalin perfusions. The implied lesson for connectomics is not to tune protocols only on appearance or CT.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed technical report; n is small (three human, two canine conditions in the abstract). ‘Adequate or favorable’ macroscopic/radiological scores are qualitative. Comparison NBF cases are previously reported, not a fully matched new control series in the truncated extract. No synapse-level connectome is attempted on these samples.

plain_language_summary: Flushing a brain with fixative can look successful from the outside or on a scan and still ruin the fine structure needed for wiring diagrams. This technical report shows that extra dehydrating chemicals can cause that mismatch.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric CLEM can place molecular cell types onto EM-reconstructable circuits, but only if labels enter tissue without detergents that destroy membranes.
ocar.challenge: Suitable small affinity reagents for detergent-free labeling are scarce relative to the biomarker lists coming from single-cell transcriptomics.
ocar.action: Lu, Wu, Li, Fang, Schalek, Su, Carter, Gupta, Jain, Janjic, and Lichtman introduce CAptVE: slow off-rate modified aptamers (SOMAmers) for fluorescent labeling on ultrastructurally reconstructable EM. The catalog paper is Nature Communications (2026); the supplied extract is the 18 September 2023 bioRxiv preprint of the same title and core author list.
ocar.resolution: The preprint reports detergent-free SOMAmer labeling, including Cy5 anti-GFP aptamers in GIN mouse cortex, and argues aptamer size (~16 kDa) is nanobody-like. CAptVE is presented as a path to integrate molecular analysis into volumetric EM and connectomics. A SomaScan comparison in the supplement notes reduced binding after aldehyde fixation for most targets.
ocar.future_work: Expanding the reagent panel after fixation, and applying CAptVE at connectomic scale, remain the stated aims. Readers should check the 2026 journal version for methods that may have changed after the 2023 preprint.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopy usually cannot tell you a cell’s molecular type. This method uses small DNA-like aptamer labels that glow under light microscopy without soap that would wreck the membranes needed for EM.
summaries.intermediate: Lu et al. present CAptVE, detergent-free labeling with SOMAmer reagents for correlated aptamer-assisted volumetric EM. The catalog entry is Nature Communications (2026); the PDF extract is bioRxiv 10.1101/2023.09.18.558240 (same title). They motivate the method by the limits of inferring molecular type from EM alone and by the scarcity of small immunoprobes. Demonstrations in the preprint include anti-GFP aptamers in GIN mice. Publisher-style copy in the catalog abstract adds that the technique preserves ultrastructure for large-scale connectomics.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a 2023 preprint, not the 2026 Nature Communications PDF; title and approach match the catalog paper, so summaries use the preprint plus catalog abstract, with the version mismatch noted. Author lists differ slightly (catalog includes Berger, Lynch, Schneider, Lichtman spelling variants). Fixation reduced SOMAmer binding for 95.2% of selected SomaScan targets in a supplementary comparison; 481 targets remained above 3× background. Not a dense connectome release.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams from electron microscopy usually cannot tell you a cell’s molecular type. This method uses small DNA-like aptamer labels that glow under light microscopy without soap that would wreck the membranes needed for EM.

ocar.opportunity: Many biological questions need nanometer EM of sparse targets inside specimens too large to image exhaustively at full resolution.
ocar.challenge: Traditional serial-section EM forces a choice between broad context and ultrastructural detail; exhaustive high-resolution acquisition is prohibitive.
ocar.action: Chandok, Patel, Wu, Berger, Schalek, Lichtman, Samuel, and Meirovitch, in a June 2026 bioRxiv preprint, introduce random-access electron microscopy (RAEM): a lower-resolution 3D survey, then physically revisited high-resolution imaging at selected sites by linking reconstructed coordinates to electron-beam positions on the original sections.
ocar.resolution: Demonstrations include vesicle-resolved synaptic boutons in human cortex, targeted imaging of more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical imaging of a nematode nervous system, and retrospective targeting in a published petabyte-scale human cortical volume. They argue ssEM becomes query-driven and multi-resolution, including on single-beam SEM, building on prior SmartEM work.
ocar.future_work: Discussion proposes registering light microscopy into the RAEM frame for correlative targeting, treating mapped volumes as shared resources, and extending SmartEM from 2D section-wise to 3D computationally guided acquisition. A patent application is noted.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopy at full detail is too slow for whole large samples. RAEM first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the microscope back only to the spots that matter, like selected synapses or mitochondria.
summaries.intermediate: Chandok et al. (bioRxiv, posted 23 June 2026) describe RAEM, a revisitable multi-resolution ssEM framework. After a low-resolution 3D survey, human or AI knowledge guides high-resolution reimaging at mapped physical sites. Applications named in the abstract are vesicle-resolved human cortical boutons, more than one million human cortical mitochondria, hierarchical nematode nervous-system imaging, and retrospective targeting of a published petabyte-scale human cortical volume. Related prior work is SmartEM, which rescanned pixels within a single field of view.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint; Harvard patent filing is disclosed. ‘More than one million’ mitochondria is the abstract’s figure; accuracy and completeness metrics for each demonstration should be checked in figures not fully captured here. Repeated-dose tolerance is reported as no detectable degradation in their experiments, not a general limit. Catalog datasets tag includes C. elegans, consistent with the nematode demonstration.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopy at full detail is too slow for whole large samples. RAEM first takes a coarser 3D survey, then sends the microscope back only to the spots that matter, like selected synapses or mitochondria.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans offers complete developmental lineages and whole-animal connectomes for both sexes, so sexual dimorphism can be dissected at cell-by-cell resolution.
ocar.challenge: Most worm neurobiology has focused on hermaphrodites; male-specific neurons, synapses, and internal-state modulation were historically understudied relative to that convenience.
ocar.action: Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (April 2026), review recent male C. elegans work and organize sexual dimorphism into three overlapping principles.
ocar.resolution: First, sex modulates lineage, neurogenesis, and fate to produce sex-specific neurons and structures. Second, sex changes synaptic topology of circuits. Third, sex acts as internal state, developmentally and dynamically modulating shared neurons. Together these program sex-specific behaviors, tune shared behaviors, and implement dimorphic plasticity. Sex-determination mechanisms differ across species, but the authors argue the principles are likely conserved.
ocar.future_work: Outlook calls for molecular mechanisms linking the sex-determination hierarchy to developmental timing and cell identity, and for connecting those effects to behavior. No new data were generated (data-availability statement).

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite worms do not have identical nervous systems. This review sorts the differences into three ideas: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different physiological ‘mode’.
summaries.intermediate: Portman, Bainbridge, Ward, and Zhang (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2026) review sexual dimorphism in the C. elegans nervous system, especially recent male neurobiology. They group effects into sex-specific cell classes, sexually dimorphic connectivity, and sex as a modulator of shared-neuron physiology. These are tied to sex-specific and sex-shared behaviors and to dimorphic plasticity. The extract is an HHS author manuscript of the April 2026 article (doi 10.1016/j.conb.2026.103175).
summaries.advanced: Opinion/review, not a primary connectome paper. Conservation across species is explicitly a hypothesis despite different sex-determination mechanisms. For comprehensive coverage the authors point to earlier reviews [1–6]. PMC author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite worms do not have identical nervous systems. This review sorts the differences into three ideas: extra cell types in one sex, different wiring, and the same cells running in a different physiological ‘mode’.

ocar.opportunity: Data-driven spiking networks can test brain computation at cellular resolution, but mammalian models are huge, statistically wired, and slower than real time.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian SNNs often infer topology statistically, obscure region-specific function, and require large computers.
ocar.action: Nanami, Yamada, Someya, Hige, Kazama, and Kohno, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2024), build a lightweight qualitative SNN of the Drosophila olfactory system with topology taken from connectome data, and implement it on a small FPGA.
ocar.resolution: The FPGA simulation ran in real time, reproduced olfactory associative learning, and reproduced characteristic spiking of different neuron types. They present the pipeline as a general method for building SNNs from biological data that can scale with dedicated hardware.
ocar.future_work: Discussion sketches an ASIC that would simulate the entire Drosophila brain at about 1 watt for insect-like robots; that chip is prospective. A bioRxiv preprint of the manuscript is noted.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly smell circuits are small enough to simulate neuron by neuron. This team built a lightweight spiking model from the fly connectome and ran it in real time on a small custom chip.
summaries.intermediate: Nanami et al. (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2024) describe a data-driven spiking neuronal network of the Drosophila olfactory system. Network topology is taken from connectome data; neurons are qualitative models chosen to capture key dynamics. Implemented on an entry-level FPGA, the network simulated in real time and reproduced associative olfactory learning plus type-typical spiking. They contrast this with large, slower mammalian SNNs that often use statistical connectivity.
summaries.advanced: ‘Qualitative modeling’ means simplified dynamics, not biophysically complete compartments. Connectome-derived topology should be checked against which fly olfactory reconstruction was used. The ~1 W whole-brain ASIC is a discussion projection, not a device in this paper. Recording data for LN and KC acknowledgements come from collaborators Seki and Inada.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly smell circuits are small enough to simulate neuron by neuron. This team built a lightweight spiking model from the fly connectome and ran it in real time on a small custom chip.

ocar.opportunity: Hunger must keep aversive learning available even while the same dopaminergic system is inhibited so that food-seeking memories can be expressed.
ocar.challenge: In Drosophila, hunger inhibits aversively reinforcing dopaminergic neurons (DANs) via dNPF, which could undermine shock- or bitter-reinforced learning if uncompensated.
ocar.action: Meschi, Duquenoy, Otto, Dempsey, and Waddell, in Neuron (2024), combine behavior, endocrine manipulations, connectomics, and physiology to trace adipokinetic hormone (AKH) effects on aversive reinforcement.
ocar.resolution: Chronic hunger mildly enhances aversive learning; satiated-baseline and hunger-enhanced learning require AKH. AKH acts via its receptor in four ventral-brain neurons, two octopaminergic. Those neurons sit upstream of ascending cells that feed aversively reinforcing DANs; octopaminergic modulation of at least SEZON01 is required for shock- and bitter-reinforced learning. Coordinated input enhancement is proposed to compensate hunger-directed DAN inhibition. Recordings of PPL101 showed reduced baseline DA and enhanced shock-evoked release when hungry.
ocar.future_work: The discussion treats compensation as network homeostasis that preserves reinforcer function during motivational DAN suppression; further sites of AKH action and bitter-tolerance mechanisms are noted as related but not fully mapped here.

summaries.beginner: Hungry flies still need to learn what to avoid, even while hunger quiets some dopamine neurons so they will seek food. This study finds a hormone pathway that turns up incoming signals to keep punishment learning working.
summaries.intermediate: Meschi et al. (Neuron, 2024) show that adipokinetic hormone supports aversive learning in hungry Drosophila. AKH receptor in four SEZ neurons (two octopaminergic) influences ascending pathways onto aversively reinforcing DANs. Connectomics places those neurons upstream of several ascending classes; SEZON01 output and octopaminergic modulation are required for shock- and bitter-reinforced learning. They propose enhanced input compensates hunger-dependent DAN inhibition (dNPF), a form of network homeostasis. The extract is a Europe PMC author manuscript of the 17 July 2024 article.
summaries.advanced: Animals are Drosophila; DAN class emphasis includes PPL101. ‘Mildly enhances’ aversive learning is the paper’s wording, not a numeric effect size in the extract. Connectomic wiring is used to generate circuit hypotheses tested with genetics and physiology. Author manuscript; present address for Otto is Münster.

plain_language_summary: Hungry flies still need to learn what to avoid, even while hunger quiets some dopamine neurons so they will seek food. This study finds a hormone pathway that turns up incoming signals to keep punishment learning working.

ocar.opportunity: Experimental stroke models differ in lesion size and location; a mesoscale rat connectome could predict which remote regions, such as hippocampus, lose function even when not directly infarcted.
ocar.challenge: How motor and spatial-memory impairments map onto connectivity change at neuronal-population and parcellation scales was unresolved across MCAO and hemorrhage models.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Wang, Kanoke, Rabiller, and Liu, in PLoS ONE (2024), combine two middle-cerebral-artery occlusion models and one intracerebral hemorrhage model with behavior, Fos hippocampal activation, and graph analysis on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome, plus dynamic coactivation modeling.
ocar.resolution: Functional impairment correlated with both extent and location of injury. Lesioned regions coactivated more with motor and spatial-learning regions than with other intact nodes. Weighted bilateral dynamic modeling detected altered hippocampal signal propagation in all three stroke types, predicting hippocampal hypoactivation and spatial-learning/memory impairment. Structural analyses describe changed hub importance that differs by model (dMCAO, ICH, sMCAO).
ocar.future_work: The paper offers an analytical framework for predicting remote diaschisis-like effects; generalization beyond these three rat models is not claimed.

summaries.beginner: A stroke in one place can silence far-away brain areas that were never directly damaged. This rat study uses a whole-brain connection map to predict those remote effects, especially in the hippocampus.
summaries.intermediate: Schmitt et al. (PLoS ONE, 2024) study two MCAO models and one ICH model in rats, measuring motor and spatial memory function and hippocampal Fos. They analyze connection similarities, graph and spatial distances, and regional importance on the neuroVIISAS rat connectome, then run dynamic coactivation models. Impairment tracked lesion extent and location; dynamic modeling predicted hippocampal hypoactivation across all three stroke types. Conclusion boxes list model-specific hub shifts (for example thalamic nuclei after dMCAO; hypothalamic and raphe nodes after ICH/sMCAO).
summaries.advanced: This is a mesoscale atlas-based connectome (neuroVIISAS), not synapse-resolution EM. Fos is a proxy for hippocampal activation. Dynamic-model predictions should be read as in silico signal propagation, constrained by the empirical lesions and behavior. Data are on figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.26197718.v1).

plain_language_summary: A stroke in one place can silence far-away brain areas that were never directly damaged. This rat study uses a whole-brain connection map to predict those remote effects, especially in the hippocampus.

ocar.opportunity: If axons from co-active ensembles land as dendritic clusters, single neurons could use dendritic nonlinearities to decode those patterns—even without special wiring rules.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether random feedforward connectivity is enough to produce such clusters, or whether brains need activity-dependent targeting.
ocar.action: Somashekar and Bhalla, in a bioRxiv preprint (November 2024 version), combine theory and simulations using rat hippocampal and cortical network statistics.
ocar.resolution: Clustered convergence of axons from 3–4 different co-active ensembles is likely even in random networks, representing arbitrary input combinations in at least ten neurons in a 100,000-cell population. With larger ensembles, spatiotemporally ordered convergence of 3–5 axons is also likely. Clusters yield higher activation when dendritic nonlinearities are strong and background activity is low. They conclude clustered/sequence computation is pervasive, but somatic selectivity needs the right physiology, background, and connectomics together.
ocar.future_work: They discuss testing predictions in EM, viral, and barcoding connectomes, and work an olfactory-bulb-to-piriform example with roughly 40 co-active mitral cells per receptor class as a structurally defined ensemble.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells might read combinations of incoming messages if those inputs land close together on a dendrite. This modeling paper argues that even random wiring is often enough to create those clusters.
summaries.intermediate: Somashekar and Bhalla (bioRxiv, posted 9 November 2024) ask whether random feedforward connectivity can cluster axons from co-active ensembles onto dendrites. Using rat hippocampal and cortical statistics, they find 3–4-ensemble clusters are likely, with at least ten representing neurons in a 100,000-cell population, and 3–5-axon sequences given larger ensembles. Expression at the soma requires strong dendritic nonlinearities and low background. They treat this as a bridge from structural connectivity to dendritic computation without invoking special targeting.
summaries.advanced: Theory and simulation, not new EM. Ensemble sizes (~100 for groups, ~1000 for sequences in the discussion) and population size (100,000) are modeling assumptions based on cited statistics. ‘At least ten’ target neurons is the abstract’s lower bound. Olfactory piriform application uses literature mitral-cell counts (~20 per glomerulus, two glomeruli per class). Unreviewed preprint.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells might read combinations of incoming messages if those inputs land close together on a dendrite. This modeling paper argues that even random wiring is often enough to create those clusters.

ocar.opportunity: Temperature reorganizes daily activity and sleep, but how the central circadian circuit encodes temperature and routes it to locomotion versus sleep was unclear.
ocar.challenge: About 150 Drosophila clock neurons interact with temperature and light; identifying the most temperature-sensitive nodes and their downstream split is hard without combined imaging, tracing, and behavior.
ocar.action: Li, Li, Yuan, Tian, Ye, Zeng, Li, and Guo, in Nature Communications (2024), use in vivo two-photon imaging with a Peltier temperature controller, trans-synaptic tracing, connectome analysis, and behavior in Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: DN1as are identified as the most sensitive temperature-sensing circadian neurons, with responses gated by the clock. They bidirectionally target activity-related E cells (LNds) and sleep-promoting DN3s. The DN1a–E circuit modulates the evening locomotion peak in cold, and the DN1a–DN3 circuit controls warm-induced nocturnal sleep reduction. Upstream inputs include TPN-II (low temperature) and TPN-IV (high temperature).
ocar.future_work: Molecular paths from clock proteins to DN1a temperature sensitivity (receptors, excitability, ER calcium) remain open. Different DN3 subpopulations may use distinct transmitters/receptors.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies change walking and sleep when the temperature changes, on top of their daily clock. This study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and then push one downstream path for evening movement and another for nighttime sleep.
summaries.intermediate: Li et al. (Nature Communications, 2024) image the Drosophila central circadian circuit during controlled temperature steps. DN1as emerge as the most temperature-sensitive neurons, clock-gated, and they innervate E cells/LNds and DN3s. Behavior assigns cold-evening locomotion to DN1a–E and warm-night sleep loss to DN1a–DN3. Connectome-consistent upstream thermosensory projection neurons (TPN-II and TPN-IV) supply low- and high-temperature information. The authors frame this as a conserved logic for integrating temperature and light across the day.
summaries.advanced: Two-photon calcium imaging with a custom Peltier device; ‘most sensitive’ is relative to the imaged circadian set, not every neuron in the brain. Bidirectional targeting is anatomical plus functional imaging and behavior. Molecular clock gating of DN1a is proposed, not fully dissected. Publisher extra abstract sentence restates the DN1a result.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies change walking and sleep when the temperature changes, on top of their daily clock. This study finds a pair of clock cells that feel temperature and then push one downstream path for evening movement and another for nighttime sleep.

ocar.opportunity: Instance segmentation of neurons in volumetric light microscopy would let labs jointly analyze morphology and function, but public real-world benchmarks for long, thin, interwoven processes are lacking.
ocar.challenge: Neurons are thin, long-range, and tightly interweaved; light-microscopy noise, partial volume, and uneven illumination break both local disentangling and long-range tracing. ML methods for long-range dependence are often scored on synthetic data.
ocar.action: Mais, Hirsch, Managan, Kandarpa, Rumberger, Reinke, Maier-Hein, Ihrke, and Kainmüller, at CVPR (2024; extract is arXiv:2404.00130), release the FlyLight Instance Segmentation Benchmark (FISBe) with pixel-wise annotations, task-specific metrics, and three baselines.
ocar.resolution: FISBe is presented as the first public multi-neuron light-microscopy dataset with pixel-wise instance labels, from Drosophila FlyLight/MCFO imagery. Baselines include PatchPerPix, Flood Filling Networks, and Duan et al. color clustering; qualitative examples show merges, splits, and coverage failures typical of the difficulty. Metrics are designed for downstream analyses.
ocar.future_work: They invite methods that capture long-range dependencies (e.g. state-space models, continuous CNNs) and self-supervised pretraining on the large unlabeled FlyLight corpus.

summaries.beginner: Computers still struggle to separate individual neurons in 3D light-microscope images, where thin branches tangle together. This paper releases a fruit-fly brain dataset with careful labels so algorithms can be scored fairly.
summaries.intermediate: Mais et al. (CVPR 2024; arXiv extract 29 March 2024) introduce FISBe, a FlyLight instance-segmentation benchmark of volumetric multi-color light microscopy of Drosophila neurons with pixel-wise ground truth. They define application-oriented metrics and provide three baselines: PatchPerPix, Flood Filling Networks (with a partial variant), and Duan et al.’s color clustering. The challenge is framed as real-world long-range thin-filament instance segmentation, unlike synthetic benchmarks. Project page: kainmueller-lab.github.io/fisbe (abstract also prints jisbe).
summaries.advanced: The extract is the arXiv camera-ready-style PDF; CVPR DOI is the catalog identifier. Baseline metric tables are dense (F1 variants, ERL-like scores) and should be read from the paper rather than a single headline number. Dataset is light microscopy, not EM. Catalog journal field is the conference name.

plain_language_summary: Computers still struggle to separate individual neurons in 3D light-microscope images, where thin branches tangle together. This paper releases a fruit-fly brain dataset with careful labels so algorithms can be scored fairly.

ocar.opportunity: Local EM connectomes and MRI-scale projectomes live at different resolutions; synthesizing axons that are spatially embedded in the whole brain could link them for in silico experiments.
ocar.challenge: Dendrites have been synthesized more successfully than long-range axons that must traverse many regions with realistic morphology and connectivity.
ocar.action: Petkantchin, Berchet, Peng, Markram, and Kanari, in Nature Communications (2025; received 2024), generate whole-brain axonal morphologies for cortical pyramidal cells from sparse experimental reconstructions, then build projectome and connectome predictions.
ocar.resolution: Computationally generated axons are reported to reproduce local and global morphological properties of experimental reconstructions and to yield large-scale inter-regional connectivity. Touches are detected by proximity, filtered by bouton interval, pruned to physiological synapse density, and converted to synapses. Data and code are released (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.13790069; BlueBrain axon-projection).
ocar.future_work: The method is for pyramidal cells in cortex as stated in the PDF; extending cell types and validating predicted long-range synapses against new experiments remain implied next steps.

summaries.beginner: We can map tiny local wiring with electron microscopy, but not every long-distance axon in a mammal. This paper grows realistic computer copies of those long axons from a smaller set of real reconstructions to estimate whole-brain connections.
summaries.intermediate: Petkantchin et al. (Nature Communications, 2025) synthesize whole-brain axonal morphologies for cortical pyramidal cells from sparse experimental reconstructions (including EM-scale local data and larger imaging). Generated axons match reported local and global morphological statistics and are used to predict inter-regional projectome and connectome structure for in silico experiments. The catalog lists bioRxiv/2024; the extract is the published 9 July 2025 article with the same title. Related NeuroTS/ROOTS literature is discussed as prior art limited in scale or region.
summaries.advanced: Synthetic connectivity, not an empirically complete EM brain. Pyramidal-cell focus is explicit in the PDF (catalog abstract is slightly more general). Synapse creation uses proximity plus density pruning (ref. 2 in the paper). Catalog year 2024 vs publication 2025. Check Zenodo contents for which species/atlas was used.

plain_language_summary: We can map tiny local wiring with electron microscopy, but not every long-distance axon in a mammal. This paper grows realistic computer copies of those long axons from a smaller set of real reconstructions to estimate whole-brain connections.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-resolution fly connectomes across development make it possible to test how connection probability scales with physical distance, a geometric constraint on brain topology.
ocar.challenge: Coarse-grained brain networks had been described with an exponential distance rule; whether synapse-level connectivity follows the same rule, and whether any scaling is functionally special, was open.
ocar.action: Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan, in Physical Review Letters (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, analyze fruit-fly synapse-resolution connectomes at different developmental stages.
ocar.resolution: The abstract reports a consistent power-law scaling of neuronal connection probability with spatial distance, distinct from the exponential distance rule of coarser networks. The scaling is said to align with maximum-entropy communication and a critical balance of integration and segregation; perturbing the probability model’s parameters or type removes those properties. An explicit predictor using only interneuronal distance and in/out degrees is derived.
ocar.future_work: How the geometric law generalizes beyond the fly datasets used is outside the abstract.

summaries.beginner: In fruit-fly brains mapped down to synapses, neurons that sit closer together are more likely to connect, following a regular geometric rule. This paper argues that rule is not just packing, but part of how the network balances mixing and separating information.
summaries.intermediate: Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan (Physical Review Letters, 2024) study synapse-resolution Drosophila connectomes across developmental stages. According to the catalog abstract, connection probability versus distance follows a power law unlike the exponential distance rule of coarse-grained networks, with claimed links to maximum-entropy communication and functional criticality. A quantitative connectivity predictor uses only distance and in/out degree. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Zhang and Tang, a 2025/2026 PNAS-style paper on heavy-tailed update distributions in nonequilibrium learning of artificial networks, not the PRL geometric-scaling connectome paper. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Physical Review Letters article is required for methods, fly datasets, and figures.

plain_language_summary: In fruit-fly brains mapped down to synapses, neurons that sit closer together are more likely to connect, following a regular geometric rule. This paper argues that rule is not just packing, but part of how the network balances mixing and separating information.

ocar.opportunity: Lightsheet whole-mouse-brain volumes are terabytes acquired in about a day, but they have little scientific value until cells are reconstructed as accurate 3D skeletons.
ocar.challenge: Prior reconstruction tools are described as disk-bound, dense-access, coupled, single-threaded, and topologically inaccurate, forcing cropped windows and heavy proofreading.
ocar.action: Marrett, Moradi, Park, Yan, Choi, Zhu, Akram, Nanda, Xue, Mun, Gutierrez, Rudd, Zingg, Magat, Wijaya, Dong, Yang, and Cong, in a bioRxiv preprint (July 2024 version), present Gossamer/Recut: ordered specializations of search that cut memory so a mouse brain can be processed in memory on one server.
ocar.resolution: They report progressively lowering memory by four orders of magnitude, processing one mouse brain in-memory, at 67× the scale with 870× less memory and 78% higher automated yield than APP2. Reconstruction is split into conversion, seed segmentation, branch segmentation, and skeletonization. Example timing on their system is 66 minutes for a demonstration workload (not the whole-brain figure).
ocar.future_work: Artifact notes recommend very large RAM (they mention 4 TB class machines) to keep whole-brain workloads in memory; lowering thread count trades speed for RAM. Proofreading remains needed for scientific-grade labels.

summaries.beginner: A whole mouse brain scanned with lightsheet microscopy is too big for older tracing programs. Gossamer is software that rebuilds neurons as 3D stick figures using far less computer memory, so one machine can handle a full brain.
summaries.intermediate: Marrett et al. (bioRxiv, posted 4 July 2024) describe Gossamer (implementation Recut) for scaling image processing and neuronal reconstruction to whole mouse brains. By recasting vision steps as ordered search, they report four orders of magnitude less memory, in-memory processing of one mouse brain, 67× scale and 870× less memory versus APP2, with 78% higher automated yield. The pipeline covers encoding, soma seeds, long-range branches, and curve skeletons. Lightsheet acquisition of a mouse brain in one day (~terabytes) is the motivating data type.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. Scale/memory/yield ratios are author-reported versus APP2; check tables for topology metrics (DIADEM etc.). ‘1 mouse brain’ in-memory assumes high-RAM hardware described in the artifact appendix. Software page: github.com/UCLA-VAST/recut. Catalog title is Gossamer; the extract also names Recut as the package.

plain_language_summary: A whole mouse brain scanned with lightsheet microscopy is too big for older tracing programs. Gossamer is software that rebuilds neurons as 3D stick figures using far less computer memory, so one machine can handle a full brain.

ocar.opportunity: Large volume-EM datasets need organelle segmentation, spatial analysis, and 3D visualization that a typical life-science lab can run on one workstation without heavy annotation.
ocar.challenge: Users with modest computational expertise face a jumble of incompatible open-source tools and costly manual labeling for each organelle class.
ocar.action: Müller, Schmidt, Albrecht, Rieckert, Otto, Galicia Garcia, Fabig, Solimena, and Weigert, in Nature Protocols (2024), as described in the catalog abstract, present a modular pipeline using Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, and Album-wrapped Python tools (CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, Jupyter).
ocar.resolution: The protocol is aimed at choosing organelle-suited segmentation tools, bridging software compatibility via Album solutions, and producing 3D labels, spatial interaction analyses, and renderings of large vEM datasets. It is a methods protocol, not a new biological dataset.
ocar.future_work: Labs must still match tools to organelle type; the abstract presents the pipeline as a reference for similar single- or multiple-organelle projects on single-user hardware.

summaries.beginner: Volume electron microscopy produces huge 3D pictures of cells, but turning them into labeled organelles is hard for non-programmers. This protocol strings together free tools so a lab computer can segment, measure, and display those structures.
summaries.intermediate: Müller et al. (Nature Protocols, 2024) describe an annotation-efficient pipeline for organelle-specific segmentation, spatial analysis, and visualization of volume EM on a standard workstation. Named tools include Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, and Album to install CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, and Jupyter notebooks. The protocol covers raw-data preparation through 3D rendering and is written for life scientists with modest computational expertise. Summaries here follow the catalog abstract because the associated PDF extract is a different article.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Adhinarta et al., VesiclePy (PLoS Computational Biology, 2026), a vesicle-analysis toolbox, not the Müller et al. Nature Protocols pipeline. Claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Independent reading of the Nature Protocols paper is required for timings, organelle examples, and software versions.

plain_language_summary: Volume electron microscopy produces huge 3D pictures of cells, but turning them into labeled organelles is hard for non-programmers. This protocol strings together free tools so a lab computer can segment, measure, and display those structures.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes give exact synapse locations on identified neurons, so one can test how topography—not just synapse count—shapes dendritic integration.
ocar.challenge: In fly looming circuits, retinotopic visual projection neurons (VPNs) synapse onto descending neurons (DNs), but whether synapses stay retinotopic on the dendrite and how that affects encoding was unknown.
ocar.action: Moreno-Sanchez, Vasserman, Jang, Hina, von Reyn, and Ausborn, in an April 2024 bioRxiv preprint, map VPN→DN synapse topography in Drosophila and build multicompartment DN models fitted to physiology using EM morphologies and synapse locations.
ocar.resolution: Synapses of a given VPN type occupy non-overlapping territories on DN dendrites but are near-random within those clusters, not retinotopic. DN dendrite morphologies normalize individual EPSP amplitudes; near-random placement yields linear encoding of synapse numbers from individual VPNs. They propose linear encoding of synapse count as a default from connectivity plus passive properties, on which active conductances and plasticity can later tune.
ocar.future_work: Supplements locate the spike initiation zone downstream of the tether in DNp01, DNp02, and DNp06 using para labeling; active properties and plasticity are left as subsequent tuners of the default linear regime.

summaries.beginner: In the fly, looming-sensitive cells dump synapses onto big descending neurons that drive escape. This preprint finds those synapses sit in type-specific neighborhoods but are shuffled inside them, which helps the cell add up synapse numbers linearly.
summaries.intermediate: Moreno-Sanchez et al. (bioRxiv, posted 28 April 2024) use Drosophila EM connectomics of looming VPN→DN circuits. Each VPN type occupies a non-overlapping dendritic territory on DNs; within a territory, synapses are near random rather than retinotopic. Multicompartment models with EM morphology and synapse locations, fitted to experimental data, show dendritic anatomy normalizes single-synapse EPSPs and that random-within-cluster placement supports linear encoding of VPN synapse counts. The framing is a default linear strategy from passive integration.
summaries.advanced: Unreviewed preprint. ‘Near random’ is relative to retinotopy within a type’s territory, not a claim of unstructured biology. Models are fitted to physiology; figure supplements on SIZ location use para-GFSTF. Which DN types (DNp01, DNp03, etc.) carry each result should be read from figures. Passive-property emphasis means active conductances are not the main mechanism claimed here.
