ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation for connectomics is typically over-segmented, so experts spend large effort merging fragments into neurons.
ocar.challenge: Most proofreading tools offer visualization and merge/split but leave truncation points and candidate partners to exhaustive manual search.
ocar.action: Liu, Chen, and Chen, in IEEE ICMEW (2024), present NeuProofreader: an interactive system that extracts candidate segment pairs and predicts pairwise connectivity from morphology and EM features, then highlights top candidates in 2D and 3D views.
ocar.resolution: In a user study of 10 volunteers (6 novices, 4 FlyWire-experienced experts) tracing two neurons from the FlyTracing dataset, suggestive prompts reduced average proofreading time by 15.61%. For experts, time fell 38.77% and expected run length (ERL) rose 3.72%. Code is released on GitHub.
ocar.future_work: They present the system as applicable across connectomics datasets and species; broader benchmarks beyond FlyTracing two-neuron tasks are not in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Computers chop electron-microscope neurons into too many pieces, and people must glue them back. NeuProofreader suggests which pieces likely belong together so proofreaders spend less time searching.
summaries.intermediate: Liu, Chen, and Chen (IEEE ICMEW, 2024) describe NeuProofreader, combining connectivity prediction with interactive 2D EM and 3D mesh views. The model scores potential merges from morphology and image features and prompts the top candidates. A 10-person study on FlyTracing reported 15.61% faster proofreading overall; experts (n = 4) were 38.77% faster with a 3.72% ERL increase. They contrast this with tools that only visualize and merge without ranking partners.
summaries.advanced: Workshop paper; user study is small (10 people, two neurons). Time and ERL percentages are those stated. Novices had no prior tracing experience; experts had FlyWire experience. Code URL in the catalog abstract has a possible typo (liuyx599I vs typical GitHub paths)—verify the repository. Licensed reprint stamp shows Johns Hopkins download.

plain_language_summary: Computers chop electron-microscope neurons into too many pieces, and people must glue them back. NeuProofreader suggests which pieces likely belong together so proofreaders spend less time searching.

ocar.opportunity: A human nanoscale synaptome would be a core object for connectomics and for bounding mental capacity and disease, but its storage cost is unknown.
ocar.challenge: Published neuron and synapse counts vary widely, and a synapse can be stored at different levels of geometric detail.
ocar.action: Nowinski, in PLoS ONE (2024), defines a synapse as paired pre/post neuron and terminal identifiers with optional coordinates and radii, then estimates storage for three models (topologic, point, geometric), full and simplified, across four neuron counts (30, 86, 100, 138 billion) and three synapses-per-neuron values (1,000, 10,000, 30,000)—72 cases.
ocar.resolution: Whole-brain full (simplified) storage ranges from 0.21 (0.14) PB to 28.98 (18.63) PB (topologic), 0.57 (0.32) to 78.66 (43.47) PB (point), and 0.69 (0.38) to 95.22 (51.75) PB (geometric). Cortical ranges are given from tens of TB to several PB. Even the topologic model is described as too large for many neuroscience supercomputers; Frontier can handle 86 billion neurons with 1,000–10,000 synapses per neuron. Fly and worm synaptomes are contrasted as MB and kB scale.
ocar.future_work: Hundreds of thousands of human synaptomes would push toward exabytes. The author notes networks of supercomputers or cloud storage as ways around single-machine limits, inspired by SYNAPSE synchrotron mapping efforts.

summaries.beginner: If we listed every human synapse, how much disk space would that take? This paper estimates petabytes—more than most neuroscience supercomputers can hold—depending on how many cells and how much detail you store.
summaries.intermediate: Nowinski (PLoS ONE, 2024) models the human nanoscale synaptome and estimates storage. A synapse is a pair of (neuron, terminal) pairs, optionally with coordinates and radii. Three models (topologic, point, geometric), each full or simplified, are crossed with neuron counts of 30–138 billion and 1,000–30,000 synapses per neuron (72 cases). Whole-brain estimates span roughly 0.14–95 PB depending on model and counts; cortex is smaller but still up to several PB. Frontier is cited as able to hold 86 billion neurons at 1,000–10,000 synapses per neuron.
summaries.advanced: Back-of-envelope morphology/storage study, not an empirical reconstruction. Neuron and synapse-per-neuron values are literature ranges, not new measurements. ‘First big data work’ on this estimate is the author’s claim. Drosophila (MB) and C. elegans (kB) comparisons are order-of-magnitude. Acknowledgments mention SYNAPSE and Ann-Shyn Chiang. All data are stated to lie within the article.
